cells.tense: The deep bench of your practice is holding, and something crossing the threshold is entering now.
cells.act: refine one distinction by close attention
cells.ask: Take a distinction in the work you've left blurry, and give it a short sitting of nothing but close attention — nothing else in the work touched.
cells.core:
When something new comes in through a practice you've kept long, you can take the whole of it at once: the quiet of working alone, the slow pass, the work that gets deeper instead of wider. You sort what belongs to the craft from what's drift, and you do it by paying close attention to the seam rather than by deciding anything big. The doors that open now open without being forced.

You keep the balance by refining a distinction that's gone soft, and refining only it. Sit with the part of the work where your eye is still slow, and sharpen that line by attention rather than pressure. Practice flows when the refinement serves the work and not a need to be finished, so the door gets met instead of overwhelmed. Give the sharpened distinction a short sitting and then put it down.
cells.sheetLine: Attention is how the deep craft finds its next piece.
cells.verb: deepen the craft through each pass, arriving at the threshold of real skill
cells.place: the turning point where what was outside enters the system

cells.tense: You are bracing at the threshold as if the whole structure must be ready before it has arrived.
cells.act: share the joy with the people it belongs to
cells.ask: Tell someone who has been part of this work one true good thing about it, out loud this week — not as a report, as gladness with company.
cells.core:
When something new is entering, you can push the work to be finished ahead of its own pace — more hours, more precision, more certainty, as if the next pass will close the gap the last one opened. The building starts standing in for the arrival, and the arrival thins out. What goes quiet is the simpler thing the work is actually for.

The way back is not more refining. It's the other side of you: let the gladness go out to the people it belongs to. Say one good thing out loud where it can be heard, so the news reaches them instead of staying at the bench. The work breathes again when its meaning travels to another person, and the threshold gets crossed in company rather than alone.

cells.tense: You are still standing at the old door, watching it, long after it already closed behind you.
cells.act: put the frame on the table before anyone asks
cells.ask: Say what you think this thing is in a single plain sentence, out loud or on paper, before anyone asks you to.
cells.core:
What's entering hasn't been met, and the practice already built sits behind you like something you won't turn around to face. What you have holds together, but nothing has been claimed aloud, so the next step reads as someone else's decision. The deep part of the craft has gone quiet, and the silence has started to look like patience.

What brings the pulse back is putting a frame on the table — not a case for it, the frame itself. Say in plain words what you think this is, before you're asked. Say it once. The structure you can already make comes back the moment a sentence carries it into the open where someone else can hear it.
cells.sheetLine: A plain sentence about the shape is what opens the door.

cells.tense: The pen is in your hand in a room where the writing keeps getting done.
cells.act: do the next piece at the speed you can keep for a month, not the speed you can keep for a day
cells.ask: Take the next piece of the work at the pace you could hold for a month, and notice the rhythm that keeps instead of the one that burns.
cells.core:
The deep practice is already being made, and the story you tell is that it just happened, that the discipline is simply how things are done, that the craft isn't really yours to have made. The threshold being crossed was walked to by the person now saying they only happened to be standing there. The structure has a maker, and the maker's own account has quietly dropped them out of it.

The smaller, earlier form of the same line is to move at the pace your feeling can sustain, with the will and the wish going the same direction. Take the next piece at the speed you could keep for a month. Feel the size of what you're walking into by holding your own stride to it, and keep your hand visible in the step you take.
